headline: Rhode Island orders hemp quarantine reports by 4 December
dek: Rhode Island tells hemp firms to quarantine, move or destroy over-limit THC stock and file records by 4 December, a week before the federal cap.
key_points: Rhode Island's Cannabis Control Commission issued five pages of guidance on 20 November for hemp products that will break the federal limits taking effect on 11 December.

Businesses must transfer, destroy or quarantine non-compliant stock before 11 December, file quarantine records by 4 December, and report anything handled from 4 to 11 December in a supplemental report due 11 December.
Quarantined hemp cannot be processed, sold or moved between businesses, and after 11 December it can leave quarantine only through a destruction request, unless lawmakers change the law.
Congress has not settled the federal question: a bipartisan Senate bill would keep hemp THC legal for adults 21 and over, while some senators and prevention groups want the cap with no further delay.
body: Rhode Island has given its hemp businesses a timetable that ends three weeks from now. Guidance the Cannabis Control Commission released on 20 November tells licensed hemp handlers to quarantine, transfer or destroy any product that will exceed the new federal THC limits, and to document what they have quarantined by Friday 4 December. The federal limits take effect a week later, on Friday 11 December.

The guidance, five pages long according to The Marijuana Herald, turns a federal change into a set of state compliance steps. It is the second time the commission has acted: in September it told licensees to get over-limit products out of their facilities before 11 December. The new document says what happens to stock that is still on the shelf.
## What the commission now requires

The guidance covers two kinds of product, according to The Marijuana Herald's reading of it. Finished hemp products sold to consumers may hold no more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container. Intermediate hemp products, meaning bulk flower, biomass, concentrates and distillates not packed for retail, face a separate limit of 0.3% total THC. The commission says the restrictions apply after harvest and do not change the federal rules on growing hemp.

Before 11 December, a business holding non-compliant product has three options: transfer it, destroy it or quarantine it. Quarantined product is frozen. It cannot be processed, manufactured, distributed or sold, and business-to-business transfers are also barred. Quarantine records are due on 4 December. Anything a business handles between 4 and 11 December goes into a supplemental report, due on 11 December itself. Mistakes can be reconciled through the commission's hemp compliance office.

After 11 December, the door narrows further. Quarantined product can be released only through a request to the Cannabis Office to destroy it, unless lawmakers change the law. Licensed marijuana businesses may ask for authority to take in hemp-derived ingredients, but only ingredients that meet the federal limits.
Some things do not change. Certificates of analysis that have already been issued remain valid, and testing methods stay the same, the commission said.
> The real deadline in Rhode Island is 4 December. After 11 December, quarantined hemp has only one way out: destruction.
## How the September order set this up

The commission first moved on 11 September, in Cannabis Office Bulletin 2026-7, The Marijuana Herald reported at the time. It cited Section 781 of the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act of 2026, which from 11 December bars hemp-derived products that are made, processed, distributed, advertised or sold at retail, online included, from containing more than 0.4 milligrams of total THC per container.

That bulletin said over-limit products could not be moved into the regulated marijuana market through an external transfer request, and could not be relabelled and sold as marijuana, whatever testing method was used. Over-limit products also had to come off websites. For destruction, the commission suggested grinding plant material and mixing it with non-consumable waste so that at least half of the mixture is non-cannabis material, then taking it to a licensed solid waste facility. Businesses can ask the Cannabis Office to watch and document the process.

The September bulletin applied to licensed hemp handlers, dual licensees, and hemp-derived consumable CBD distributors and retailers. Products at or under the 0.4 milligram line stay under Rhode Island's existing hemp licensing rules.
## The federal fight is still open

The 11 December date was not the original one. The ban was first set for November and was pushed back to 11 December, WRAL reported on 18 November. As we reported on 12 November, a first phase covering synthetic hemp products has already taken effect.

On Capitol Hill, Sen. Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.) and Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) have introduced the Hemp Guardrails Act, which would keep hemp-derived THC legal for adults 21 and older under new safety rules, according to WRAL. Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.) answered on X that he would never support it, calling the hemp market an industry that should never have existed. As we reported on 14 November, Sen. Pete Ricketts (R-Neb.) has also argued against any further delay.

Outside Congress, prevention groups are pressing the same way. In a 17 November release, Every Brain Matters and Citizens for a Safe and Healthy Texas urged Congress and the President to keep the 0.4 milligram per-container limit with no exemptions or delays.

The stakes are large in some states. North Carolina ranks sixth in the nation for supplying hemp THC products, with sales of nearly $2 billion in 2025, WRAL reported, citing a March 2026 market assessment. WRAL set out four paths: the ban takes effect; Congress passes the Sheehy-Klobuchar bill; another delay into next year; or states keep their own rules and in effect ignore the federal change.
## What it means for operators

For Rhode Island businesses, the guidance removes the option of waiting to see what Congress does. A business that holds over-limit stock on 4 December must have recorded it, and stock still in quarantine after 11 December can only be destroyed under current law. If Congress does act before 11 December, the guidance itself says the outcome depends on lawmakers, so operators would need a fresh word from the commission before releasing anything.

For other states, Rhode Island offers a template. Its approach has three parts: an inventory snapshot a week before the deadline, a supplemental report for the final week, and a single destruction-only exit afterwards. On our reading of the timetable, that gives the regulator a full record of over-limit stock before the federal rule bites, rather than finding it during later inspections.
## What to watch
Friday 4 December: quarantine documentation is due to Rhode Island's Cannabis Office.
Friday 11 December: the federal 0.4 milligram per-container limit takes effect, along with Rhode Island's supplemental report deadline for the final week, unless Congress changes the date first.
Between now and then: any floor action on the Hemp Guardrails Act or a funding bill that carries a hemp delay, and whether more states follow Rhode Island with written quarantine rules.
